Basal metabolic rate in the brown lemur (Eulemur fulvus) has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions, revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 746 milliliters per hour [JOi = 746 milliliters per hour] when the animal's core body temperature was maintained at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This value is consistent with the relatively low metabolic demands typical of folivorous-frugivorous primates, reflecting an energy-conserving strategy that aligns with the species' seasonal feeding ecology. Gestation in Eulemur fulvus is comparatively brief for a lemur of this body size, with published accounts noting that pregnancy lasts approximately 118 days [tg = approximately 118 days] under normothermic conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a duration that falls within the lower range of the 120 to 129 day interval commonly cited in the literature. The timing of parturition is strongly linked to the onset of the rainy season in their native Madagascar, ensuring that resources are abundant when the neonate arrives. This species typically gives birth to a single offspring per litter, though twinning has occasionally been documented in captivity.

Neonatal brown lemurs emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably modest wet weight of 73 grams [Wwb = 73 grams], a diminutive size that renders the infant almost entirely dependent on maternal warmth and milk during the first weeks of life. The suckling juvenile experiences rapid mass gain over the subsequent months, driven by a lipid-rich milk composition that facilitates neural development and thermoregulatory capacity. Under the stable thermal regime of a captive setting, with ambient conditions held at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the pup attains a wet weight at weaning of 1050 grams [Wwx = 1050 grams] approximately 153 days after birth [tx = approximately 153 days after birth], which equates to roughly five months of maternal investment. This weaning weight represents a greater than fourteen-fold increase from the birth mass and signifies the completion of the most nutritionally demanding phase of early development. The transition to solid foods coincides with the eruption of the permanent dentition, allowing the juvenile to begin processing fruits and leaves independently.

The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult brown lemur is approximately 2600 grams [Wwi = approximately 2600 grams], though field studies indicate considerable individual variation, with mature individuals ranging from 2 to 4 kilograms depending on sex, season, and habitat quality. Males tend to be slightly heavier than females, a dimorphism likely linked to intrasexual competition for mating opportunities. The species exhibits a maximum reproductive rate characterized by a typical litter of 1.1 pups [N_R_i = 1.1 pups] and the capacity to produce 2 litters per year [F_R_i = 2 litters per year] when conditions are favorable and the core body temperature remains near 36.6 °C [T = near 36.6 °C]. This output is relatively modest compared to small-bodied strepsirrhines, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a diet rich in fibrous plant material. The inter-birth interval is heavily influenced by the duration of lactation, which imposes substantial energetic demands on the female and limits the frequency with which she can successfully rear successive litters.

Sexual maturation in the brown lemur occurs gradually, with individuals typically reaching puberty at approximately 509 days since birth [tp = approximately 509 days since birth] under controlled thermal environments maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This developmental milestone is marked by the onset of gonadal steroidogenesis and the emergence of adult social behaviors, including olfactory marking and agonistic displays. The age at which a female experiences her first oestrus is a critical life-history transition, as it determines the earliest opportunity for reproductive contribution to the population. Field observations suggest that the timing of first reproduction can be delayed beyond the pubertal threshold if ecological conditions are suboptimal, with females sometimes deferring breeding until they have attained a sufficient body condition to sustain gestation and lactation. This flexibility in the onset of reproduction is a common adaptation among long-lived primates that inhabit unpredictable seasonal environments, allowing individuals to buffer against resource shortfalls.

Maximum documented longevity for Eulemur fulvus in managed care settings has been recorded at just over 12,958 days [am = 12,958 days] when the animal's average body temperature remained close to 36.6 °C [T = close to 36.6 °C], a figure that corresponds to approximately 35.5 years of life and underscores the species' placement within a slow life-history continuum. This extended lifespan likely evolved as a consequence of low extrinsic adult mortality, a pattern shared with many other arboreal, group-living primates that benefit from reduced predation risk within cohesive social units. The ultimate wet weight of 2600 grams [Wwi = 2600 grams] places the brown lemur in an intermediate size class relative to other members of the Eulemur genus, with related species such as the black lemur achieving slightly heavier adult masses. The modest wet weight at birth of 73 grams [Wwb = 73 grams] appears to be a phylogenetic constraint shared across the family Lemuridae, where altricial neonates are the norm. Comparative analyses of life-history traits among Malagasy strepsirrhines indicate that the relatively slow pace of reproduction and development in Eulemur fulvus is tightly coupled with a diet dominated by mature leaves, which provide a stable but only moderately energy-dense resource base.
